channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: What is 'food is medicine'? Two experts explain this decades‑old approach to health care that is taking on new life
item.description: Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.

item.title: Cervical cancer elimination is in reach—we just need more GP appointments
item.description: For most Australians, general practice (GP) clinics are the first point of contact when seeking medical care. But many of us can relate to the difficulties of booking, paying for and attending an appointment.

item.title: Broad genomic testing linked to longer survival in advanced lung cancer, according to new study
item.description: New research in the November 2026 issue of Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network found that patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) lived longer when they received broad-based genomic sequencing (BGS)—testing a large panel of dozens or hundreds of genes at once—before starting treatment, compared with patients who received more limited biomarker testing of just one or two genes.

item.title: Perceiving greater discrimination in health care, the LGBTQIA+ community delays seeking medical appointments
item.description: People in the LGBTQ+ community face extra barriers in their daily lives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. One of the areas where these individuals sometimes suffer discrimination is in health care. In fact, a survey by the State Federation of Lesbians, Gays, Trans, Bisexual, and Intersex People found that more than 20% of the trans people surveyed had felt discriminated against when visiting primary care providers.

item.title: Young Australians are paying the price for a health system that doesn't fit their lives
item.description: Gen Z Australians are increasingly delaying health care, missing work and study, or sometimes going without care because of cost, inconvenience and difficulty accessing a general practitioner (GP). Nearly one in three have taken time off work, study or caregiving responsibilities to see a GP, while one in five delayed care because of cost in the past 12 months.

item.title: Infant mortality falls by 16% in some of England's most deprived areas, new national data show
item.description: Infant mortality in some of England's most disadvantaged areas fell by 16% from April 2025 to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the latest national data published by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) at the University of Bristol.

item.title: Molecular mapping of 8 million cells brings cerebral architecture into focus
item.description: University of California, Irvine researchers have mapped approximately 8 million cells in regions deep within the human brain, identifying 60 distinct types and revealing how they form cellular communities. The work offers a foundational reference for investigating brain systems affected by Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Cancer vaccines show promise for treatment and prevention
item.description: For more than three decades, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have pursued an ambitious idea: that vaccines could train the immune system to recognize and fight cancer. Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

item.title: Key brain area reveals distinct zones whose boundaries blur with age
item.description: Scientists in the Center for Human Brain Variation at the Broad Institute have charted previously hidden architecture and patterns of cellular makeup in a key part of the brain called the striatum, which is involved in decision-making and movement and is affected in psychiatric disorders, addiction and neurodegeneration. The findings reveal six new zones within the striatum based on gene expression patterns. They also demonstrate how the zones' boundaries blur with age and highlight ways that advancing age and genetic variation affect gene expression in the brain.

item.title: Experimental blood test detects early breast cancer and predicts recurrence
item.description: One of the great hopes of cancer medicine over the past decade has been a simple blood test that would detect cancer at its earliest stages, help physicians choose the right treatment and even predict the risk of recurrence. Known as liquid biopsies, these tests work by identifying traces of cancer cells in the bloodstream. Although they are already used to tailor treatment for some patients, they still struggle to detect cancer early in the general population or predict whether the disease will return after treatment.

item.title: Personalized mobile health coaching offers new approach to preventing gestational diabetes in high-risk pregnancies
item.description: A continuous, personalized mobile health (mHealth) coaching program can significantly reduce gestational diabetes incidence among high-risk pregnant women, independent of changes to maternal weight—according to an international study published in the Lancet Digital Health.

item.title: Organ-on-chip shows how tumors interact with nerves and blood vessels
item.description: On an organ-on-a-chip, researchers can now explore how tumors grow and interact with their surroundings. The chip, a small plate where cancer cells, nerves and blood vessels grow, was developed by researchers at Linköping University, Sweden, in collaboration with colleagues at Politecnico di Milano in Italy. It is described in an article published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

item.title: AI-powered lung cancer atlas identifies cell types linked to higher risk of spread
item.description: Recent advances in cancer biology have shown that a tumor is not a uniform mass. It consists of many different cancer cells and is embedded in an environment of immune cells, connective tissue and blood vessels. This variety is a significant factor in determining whether a tumor spreads and how well a therapy works. While single-cell approaches are considered pioneering instruments in cancer research, their translation into clinical practice has been limited to date, primarily due to a lack of large patient data sets with comprehensive clinical histories.

item.title: What spaceflight reveals about nerves and bone recovery
item.description: Mechanical loading is important for maintaining bone mass, and researchers from Science Tokyo have found that sensory nerves inside the bone play a key role in this process. In mice, sensory nerve abundance changed in response to mechanical unloading and reloading, and removing these nerves prevented bone recovery. The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

item.title: A novel pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome induced by direct stimulation of Ephrin-B1
item.description: A group led by the Department of Cell Biology at the Kidney Research Center, Niigata University, has identified a novel Ca²⁺-independent pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome. The study is published in The American Journal of Pathology.

item.title: Once considered junk, cellular 'chimeras' emerge as key to better cancer care
item.description: UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have found an answer to one of the great mysteries of human biology, and the discovery could have major implications for the battle against breast cancer and other diseases.

item.title: Pilot study tests cell therapy for difficult-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers
item.description: An experimental cell therapy was well tolerated in 10 people with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, according to a first-in-human study led by researchers at Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine (WFIRM).

item.title: Health scoring system could help reduce deaths among children with malnutrition in low-resource communities
item.description: New research co-led by the Center for Global Child Health at The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) suggests that a new tool for use in low-resource settings can save lives and reduce the need for hospital stays among children receiving outpatient treatment for malnutrition.

item.title: One-hour test could help doctors better spot memory problems
item.description: With the expected worldwide rise in all-cause dementia to approximately 152.8 million by the year 2050 and the potential for disease-modifying therapies such as anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies, there will be an increased demand on neurologists and memory clinics to rapidly identify and stage patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias. While neuropsychological assessment provides information that is essential to the patient and the clinician, substantial barriers remain, including a shortage of trained neuropsychologists, lengthy test batteries and the delayed turnaround of written reports.

item.title: Rethinking the road to cancer care in Rwanda
item.description: While studying health systems around the world during a yearlong fellowship, Abel Sapirstein traveled to northern Rwanda to visit Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence, which at the time was the country's only publicly accessible facility to offer comprehensive oncology services.

item.title: Tuberculosis rapid test allows in-the-field results
item.description: Northwestern University engineers have developed a new way to quickly test for tuberculosis that avoids several pitfalls of other methods.

item.title: Protein guides cytoneme 'highway' formation to support developmental signaling
item.description: Cytonemes are tendril-like appendages that developing cells use to communicate across large distances. Their cargo—including the key signaling protein Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—is highly specific, but the mechanisms underlying this specificity were unclear.

item.title: 7 simple self-care habits that may ease anxiety and depression
item.description: If you've been feeling more on edge lately, you're far from alone.

item.title: Mediterranean diet can help clear fat from the pancreas and improve blood-sugar control
item.description: Fat that builds up in the pancreas is one of the lesser-known risk factors for diabetes and metabolic syndrome, but it turns out it can be targeted directly through what's on the plate.

item.title: How to test whether brain organoids possess consciousness
item.description: The development of brain organoids is advancing at a breakneck pace. Researchers are creating tiny cell clusters in the lab that behave like fragments of the human brain. Whether such organoids could develop intelligence—or even consciousness—remains a matter of debate. Professor Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum, Germany, and Professor Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris propose an experimental framework to answer this question. Their article was published in a special issue on brain organoids of the journal Neuron on Nov. 11, 2026.

item.title: AHA: Pelacarsen cuts lipoprotein(a) levels but does not lower risk for major adverse cardiovascular events
item.description: For adults with preexisting cardiovascular disease, pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide administered monthly, lowers lipoprotein(a) levels but does not reduce the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events, according to a study published online Nov. 7 in the New England Journal of Medicine to coincide with the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held from Nov. 6 to 9 in Chicago.

item.title: First human model for form of inherited heart disease uses realistic levels of mutant protein
item.description: Inherited cardiomyopathies—diseases of the heart muscle, which cause the heart to have a harder time pumping blood to the rest of the body—are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM) is one such familial disease that affects approximately 1 in 2,000 individuals worldwide. No disease-specific therapies exist for DRM, with patients receiving only generic heart failure medicines.

item.title: Shopping for a 2027 health plan? State aid and 4 smart moves can cut your health costs
item.description: Residents of at least 11 states who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace can get extra state help paying their premiums in 2027.

item.title: New guidance outlines use of first immunotherapy for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
item.description: For the first time, children ages 8 to 17 who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have access to an approved treatment that targets the underlying autoimmune disease, rather than solely managing blood sugar levels with insulin.

item.title: Rare genetic discovery explains sex development differences in two XY sisters
item.description: Two young girls in Vietnam are living proof that there is a lot more to sex than genetics, after being found to have an extremely rare sexual development condition.
